title: Arjuna's Restless Mind
hook: Arjuna says the mind is like the wind; Krishna doesn't argue
carry: abhyasa: the mind is held by coming back
tomorrow: can you read a holy text on your own?

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti: God accepts what's offered with love, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, even Shabari's tasted berries. Today, back on the battlefield, Arjuna admits something most of us know.

Krishna has been describing a steady mind, still as a lamp in a place with no wind. And Arjuna, the hero, says what everyone is thinking. Krishna, the mind is restless. It's stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it still is as hard as holding the wind.
screen: `A LAMP WITH NO WIND.` → `THE MIND IS RESTLESS.` → `LIKE HOLDING THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held by two things: abhyasa and vairagya. Abhyasa is practice, coming back again and again. Vairagya is letting go, loosening the grip of wanting. Not talent, not one heroic effort: coming back, and letting go, together. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras name the very same pair. It's one of the most lived teachings in Hinduism, and you can see it on a string. A japa mala is a loop of beads, usually 108, with one larger bead marking where a round begins. With each bead you say a name of God or a short mantra: Om Namah Shivaya, or Hare Krishna, or Rama's name. The mind wanders. The next bead brings it back. That's abhyasa, in your fingers. Many teachers say the wandering isn't failure; noticing and coming home is the practice. The beads don't count perfect minutes. They count returns. Priya's own version is on a desk. At the very start of Nani's line she meets karmany, from karma, action, and two letters have fused into a knot, the r riding on top of the ma like a small hook. She wants to quit. Then she remembers Nani's mala clicking softly every morning, bead after bead, for as long as Priya can remember. Nani never waited to be good at it. She just keeps coming back.
screen: `YES, THE MIND IS RESTLESS.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK.` · `VAIRAGYA: LETTING GO.` · `A MALA: 108 RETURNS.` · then, large: `THE BEADS COUNT RETURNS.`

segments.voice: If you have a mala or a string of prayer beads, take it; if not, count on your fingers, thumb touching each joint. With each one, say softly a name of God you love, or, if you don't pray, a word that steadies you. When you notice the mind has wandered, don't scold it. Move to the next bead and come back. That return is the practice.
Devanagari: the script where karmany, from karma, the first word of Nani's line, ties two letters into one knot.
Hold on to it: abhyasa. The mind is held by coming back, bead by bead. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Japa on a mala of 108 beads is a daily practice in many Hindu homes, often early in the morning; a larger bead marks where a round begins, and many people turn the mala back there rather than cross it.

notes: Answers 1432's question. Gita 6.34 (Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind) and 6.35 (Krishna: by abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, dispassion, it is held) are paraphrased; 'letting go' stands for vairagya. Confirm.

Reph (the r riding above the next consonant) named only in the trapdoor. 'Karma' as the first word of 2.47: the text has karmaṇi (in action), written in sandhi as karmaṇy-; the lesson calls it karma for simplicity. A scholar may prefer 'karmani'. The sandhi itself is taught on day 1437.
